summary:
Vectra is a helmet heads-up display that turns NASA data into a hyper-local survival guide for the first crewed EVA in Jezero Crater, Mars. It is meant to be on the astronaut's HUD. The prototype, runs in any browser, on a Meta Quest 2 or a laptop, with nothing to install.

A Python pipeline converts real mission data into safety layers draped over true-scale HiRISE terrain: slope, roughness and no-go zones; a radio comms-shadow map built from Fresnel-zone clearance and Mars curvature; dust-devil risk by time of sol, detected in Perseverance MEDA pressure data; and a radiation dose clock based on Curiosity RAD, with a replay of the real 20 May 2024 solar storm. An A* planner finds the safest walking route from the habitat to the Three Forks sample depot and back, estimates walking time, and drives a live turn-back timer and an instant shelter re-route when a solar event hits. A minimap and Capcom, an AI voice assistant, keep the astronaut oriented and informed hands-free.

Mars maps today are global, but EVAs are local, timed and dangerous. Vectra puts the answers to "where is it safe, and when must I turn back?" inside the visor.
details:
Vectra is a helmet heads-up display (HUD) for an astronaut walking on Mars. We made a working protoype; it runs in the web browser of a Meta VR headset, or on any laptop, with nothing to install. Our scenario is the first crewed EVA in Jezero Crater: walk from the habitat to the Three Forks sample depot, where Perseverance left ten sample tubes, continue to a delta-front outcrop, and return safely.

An offline Python pipeline turns NASA data into map layers that the web app draws over real terrain:

- Terrain and hazards: a 3 km x 3 km crop of the USGS HiRISE elevation model for Jezero is rendered at true scale in VR. We compute slope and surface roughness from it and mark anything steeper than 20 degrees, or inside hand-drawn sand fields, as no-go.

- Comms shadow: we model a 400 MHz radio link from a 3 m habitat antenna to the astronaut's helmet. For every spot on the map we check whether the terrain blocks the line of sight or intrudes into the Fresnel zone, including Mars curvature. The result drives live 0-4 signal bars and a coverage overlay.

- Dust-devil risk: we filtered Perseverance MEDA pressure data to find the short pressure dips that passing dust devils cause, counted them by hour of the Martian day, and corrected for gaps in the data. The HUD shows LOW, RISING or HIGH risk for the current local solar time, and we compared our results with published Jezero research.

- Radiation: a dose clock based on Curiosity's measured surface radiation, plus a replay of the real 20 May 2024 solar particle event using NASA DONKI records.

- Route and timing: an A* path planner finds the safest route through the hazard map. A hiking-speed model adjusted for a pressure suit estimates walking time, which drives a live turn-back timer within a 6-hour EVA budget. When a solar storm hits, the HUD instantly shows the fastest path to shelter.

- Navigation and voice: a minimap keeps the astronaut oriented, and Capcom, an AI voice assistant named after mission control's capsule communicator, keeps them informed hands-free.

Today's Mars maps are global and static. An astronaut on foot needs local, live answers: Where is it safe to walk? Can I still reach the habitat by radio? Is a dust devil likely right now? How much radiation have I taken? When must I turn back? Vectra puts all of this in one view, in the place the astronaut is already looking.

Vectra is a prototype for planning and rehearsing future crewed EVAs. Teams can test routes, antenna placement and timing before anyone steps outside. The same approach of combining terrain, radio coverage, weather and timing in a HUD also fits field crews on Earth, such as desert survey and rescue teams in Qatar who work in remote, hot terrain with patchy signal.

- Languages: JavaScript (ES modules) and Python 3.11

- Web and VR: three.js, WebXR, HTML/CSS, hosted on GitHub Pages

- Data processing: NumPy, SciPy, pandas, rasterio, Pillow

- Hardware: Meta Quest 2 and laptops

- AI: AI coding assistants to speed up development (every AI-assisted file is labelled and was reviewed by a team member) and an AI voice service for Capcom

- Data: USGS HiRISE terrain, Perseverance MEDA and raw images, Curiosity RAD, NASA DONKI, NASA Mars Trek

Most Mars map projects are viewed on a flat screen. Vectra turns the map into a heads-up display you stand inside and walk through. It combines radio engineering, signal processing, space weather and path planning in one live interface. Every layer comes from real mission data, not invented values.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Safety first: no-go zones are absolute, and the turn-back timer always leaves enough time to walk home.

- Suit limits: slower walking speed, a slope limit and a fixed EVA budget.

- Communications: radio shadows behind ridges, and no real-time help from Earth because of the signal delay.

- Radiation units: baseline dose (mSv) and storm dose (µGy) are shown separately because they cannot honestly be added.

- Headset comfort: we target a smooth frame rate on the Quest 2 to avoid motion sickness, and a laptop mode serves judges without a headset.

- Honest assumptions: antenna and helmet heights, radio frequency, suit speed and detection thresholds are documented in our README. Our dust-devil count measures encounters at one spot, so it is a lower bound.
